entities.summary:
Lê Thái Tông, born Lê Nguyên Long (黎元龍) in Hanoi on December 31, 1423, ascended the throne as the second Emperor of the Lê dynasty of Đại Việt in 1433, ruling until his untimely death in 1442. His reign, though brief, was pivotal in consolidating the newly independent state following the expulsion of the Ming Chinese occupation. He inherited a kingdom grappling with the transition from wartime governance to stable imperial administration, a challenge he met by actively engaging in legislative and administrative reforms designed to centralize power and standardize the legal framework, thereby cementing the foundations laid by his father, Emperor Lê Lợi.

During his nine-year rule, Lê Thái Tông focused on strengthening the imperial bureaucracy, promoting Confucian education, and revising the legal codes. He personally oversaw the examination system, ensuring a meritocratic selection of officials, and initiated significant land reforms aimed at stabilizing peasant livelihoods and increasing state revenue. His edicts consistently sought to curb the power of regional magnates and enhance the authority of the central government. Notably, he implemented measures to standardize weights, measures, and currency, fostering economic stability and facilitating trade across Đại Việt. These policies laid crucial groundwork for the subsequent flourishing of the Lê dynasty.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Lê Thái Tông's reign was crucial for the Lê dynasty, consolidating the newly independent Đại Việt through significant administrative and legal reforms. His policies laid the groundwork for a stable state, despite the political fallout from the Lệ Chi Viên Incident.
